strengths: Novel and well-motivated synthesis of ideas: representing latent manifolds as implicit submanifolds via a learned denoising-based projection (following Alain & Bengio), combined with the time-discrete geodesic calculus of Rumpf & Wirth, yielding practical algorithms for geodesic interpolation and exponential-map extrapolation on latent spaces of arbitrary codimension.

The approach is autoencoder-agnostic and metric-agnostic (Euclidean, pullback, pullback-of-Riemannian-distance, KL/Fisher-Rao), which is demonstrated across four qualitatively different settings: isometric shell autoencoders, spherical VAEs on motion capture data, low-distortion image autoencoders, and even a purely distance-function-based manifold representation (Pose-NDF), showing good generality.

The augmented Lagrangian formulation is explicitly designed to tolerate an imperfect/inexact implicit representation ζσ, which is an important and honestly addressed practical concern (backed by citations to inexact-constraint AL theory and empirical checks in Fig. 2/3).

The appendix contains a systematic study (on the toy torus model) of how projection accuracy depends on sample size, network capacity, and noise level, lending some empirical grounding to the method's core denoising-projection component.

Convergence guarantees of the discrete geodesic/exponential map to the continuous counterparts are grounded in prior established theory (Rumpf & Wirth, 2015), giving the discrete calculus a principled basis rather than being purely heuristic.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is almost entirely qualitative (visual comparison of decoded shape/pose sequences to linear interpolation baselines); no quantitative metrics (e.g., path length, self-intersection rate, reconstruction fidelity, distance to data manifold) are reported to substantiate claims of improved realism or 'avoiding self-intersections more effectively.'

No empirical comparison against the substantial body of related work on latent-space Riemannian geometry discussed in Section 1.1 (Arvanitidis et al. 2018/2021/2022, Chen et al. 2018, Shao et al. 2018, Sun et al. 2025); only a naive linear-interpolation baseline is used, making it hard to assess whether the proposed implicit-submanifold approach actually improves over existing pullback-metric methods in practice.

Computational cost and scalability of the method (BFGS-based augmented Lagrangian per discrete geodesic, iterative solves for the exponential map) are not reported or discussed, which is relevant given that a main motivating claim is efficiency of low-dimensional latent-space computation versus expensive full shape-space operations.

Hyperparameter σ selection is only guided by rough heuristics ('choose the same σ for similar point cloud densities'), with no principled or automated selection procedure, and the paper acknowledges but does not resolve the sensitivity of the projection accuracy to this choice.

Figure 3 shows that geodesic extrapolation via the learned implicit representation diverges exponentially from the ground truth in regions of negative curvature; while honestly reported, this raises concerns about the reliability of the exponential map for extrapolation tasks in practice, and no mitigation or quantitative bound is offered beyond a qualitative remark.

The pullback-metric variant (WM) that gives the most compelling qualitative results (Section 5.2, 5.3) relies on an a priori known Riemannian structure on the data manifold (e.g., SO(3) product structure for poses, rotation angle for the cow images); for more generic high-dimensional data without such known structure, the method reduces to weaker Euclidean/near-isometric assumptions, limiting the generality of the strongest demonstrated results.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: making latent spaces of autoencoders geometrically usable for downstream Riemannian operations (geodesic interpolation/extrapolation), rather than treating them as a mere compression bottleneck.

The combination of a denoising-based approximate projection (extending Alain & Bengio 2014 to codimension-agnostic implicit manifold representation) with the time-discrete geodesic calculus of Rumpf & Wirth (2015) is a sensible and technically coherent synthesis, and the paper correctly leverages existing convergence theory (Corollary 4.10, Theorem 5.1) to justify the discretization.
The augmented Lagrangian treatment of inexact/imperfect implicit constraints is a reasonable and practically relevant adaptation, since in practice ζσ never exactly vanishes on the manifold.

Demonstrates versatility across a reasonably diverse set of autoencoders and data types (isometric autoencoder on discrete shells, spherical VAE on motion capture, low-distortion image autoencoder, and an existing neural distance field Pose-NDF), showing the framework is not tied to a specific architecture.
The related work section is thorough and clearly positions the contribution relative to pullback-metric approaches (Arvanitidis et al., Chen et al., Sun et al.) and neural implicit representations.

Toy torus experiments (section A.3) provide at least one setting with ground-truth comparison, giving some quantitative insight into how projection error scales with sample size, architecture, and noise.
weaknesses: Evaluation is almost entirely qualitative: aside from the toy torus, all 'real' examples (shells, mocap, images, Pose-NDF) are assessed only by visual inspection of decoded sequences (self-intersections, smoothness) with no quantitative metrics such as geodesic length comparisons, reconstruction/path-energy error, number/severity of self-intersections, or distance-to-manifold statistics. This makes it hard to judge how much the proposed geodesics actually improve over baselines beyond anecdotal figures.

No empirical comparison against the directly competing methods discussed at length in related work (Arvanitidis et al. 2018/2021/2022, Chen et al. 2018, Sun et al. 2025, Shao et al. 2018). The paper only argues conceptual differences but never benchmarks against them, so the practical advantage of the proposed implicit-manifold approach over pullback-metric approaches is unsubstantiated.

The core methodological ingredients (time-discrete geodesic calculus, denoising-based projection) are both adopted essentially unchanged from prior work (Rumpf & Wirth 2015; Alain & Bengio 2014); the novelty lies mainly in combining them for latent spaces, which is a relatively incremental methodological contribution.

Selection of the key hyperparameter σ is given only heuristic, qualitative guidance ('we could choose the same σ for similar point cloud densities'), with no principled procedure or sensitivity analysis on the real-data experiments (only on the toy torus).

The exponential map is shown (fig. 3) to suffer from exponentially growing divergence under small inaccuracies in the learned implicit representation, and this limitation is acknowledged but not mitigated or quantified on the real datasets, raising concern about reliability of the extrapolation results shown in figs. 6 and 7.

No discussion of computational cost/runtime/scalability of the augmented Lagrangian + BFGS pipeline relative to baseline interpolation or to directly computing geodesics in the full data/shape space, despite computational efficiency being motivated in the introduction as a key reason to work in latent space.

The SVAE experiment explicitly ignores the stochastic nature of encoder/decoder ('by a slight abuse of notation'), which is a nontrivial simplification whose impact on the validity of the resulting geometric computations is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: many architecture/training details are relegated to the appendix with some specificity, but no code availability is mentioned, and several design choices (e.g., discard of self-intersecting training pairs, choice of K, network depths per experiment) appear ad hoc and dataset-specific without justification or ablation.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of two ideas: (1) representing latent manifolds of autoencoders as implicit submanifolds via a learned denoising-based projection, and (2) a time-discrete variational geodesic calculus (building on the well-established Rumpf & Wirth framework) that is explicitly designed to be robust to the inaccuracies of such learned implicit representations. This fills a clear gap relative to prior pullback-metric approaches to latent space geometry (Arvanitidis et al., Chen et al., Shao et al., Sun et al.), which are discussed thoughtfully in related work.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper connects the discrete path-energy minimization and discrete exponential map to known convergence results (Rumpf & Wirth 2015) and gives a principled derivation of the denoising projection as a Gaussian-weighted barycenter (following Alain & Bengio), with discussion of the induced approximation error (O(σ²) interior / O(σ) boundary).

The augmented Lagrangian formulation is explicitly designed and justified (citing Frick et al., Jin) to tolerate inexact/non-vanishing implicit constraints, which is an important practical nuance that is handled carefully rather than assumed away.

Broad and diverse experimental demonstration across very different autoencoder types and data modalities: isometric autoencoder on discrete shells/SCAPE, spherical VAE on motion capture data (SO(3) poses), a low-bending/low-distortion image autoencoder, and an external pretrained neural distance field (Pose-NDF), showing the framework's generality and autoencoder-agnostic nature.

A dedicated ablation on a toy torus model (Appendix A.3) studies how projection accuracy depends on sample size, architecture size, and noise level, lending credibility to the denoising-projection design choice and giving some insight into hyperparameter behavior (σ).

Results are visually compelling: geodesic interpolation/extrapolation consistently avoids artifacts (self-intersections, unnatural limb contractions) that appear under naive linear latent-space interpolation, illustrating practical value for shape/pose interpolation tasks.
Extensive appendix with implementation and training details (architectures, optimizer settings, data generation procedures) supports reproducibility of the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Evaluation is almost entirely qualitative (visual comparison of interpolated meshes/poses/images); the paper lacks quantitative metrics (e.g., numerical geodesic distance error, measures of self-intersection/implausibility, realism scores, or convergence rates in K beyond the toy torus) that would substantiate the claimed improvements over linear interpolation and support comparisons across settings.

No direct empirical comparison against the competing latent-geometry methods discussed in related work (pullback-metric approaches of Arvanitidis et al., Chen et al., Shao et al., Sun et al.), so the practical benefit of the proposed implicit-manifold approach relative to these established alternatives is not demonstrated empirically.

Computational cost and scalability of the pipeline (augmented Lagrangian + BFGS inner solves, learning Πσ) are not reported or analyzed, which is relevant given the motivation of the paper is partly computational efficiency relative to full shape-space optimization.

Hyperparameter selection (especially σ, but also K, network depth/width) is only systematically studied on the synthetic torus example; for the real-data experiments the paper states σ was chosen heuristically ('same σ for similar point cloud densities') without a principled selection procedure or sensitivity analysis on real latent manifolds.

The exponential map is noted to diverge exponentially from ground truth under small representation errors (Fig. 3), and this instability is only characterized qualitatively; there is no quantitative bound or mitigation strategy for how large K, σ, or curvature affect reliability of extrapolation in practice.

No statement about code/data release, which, combined with the qualitative nature of the results, somewhat limits independent verification and reproducibility beyond re-implementation from the detailed but lengthy appendix.

Latent dimensions considered in experiments are all fairly modest (l between ~3 and 16, with the Pose-NDF example at l=84 only for interpolation, not projection learning), leaving open how well the denoising-projection approach and discrete calculus scale to substantially higher-dimensional or higher-codimension latent spaces typical of large modern autoencoders.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated extension of the time-discrete geodesic calculus of Rumpf & Wirth (2015) to the setting of imperfect, implicitly represented latent manifolds, addressing a genuine gap between geometric shape-space methods and autoencoder latent spaces.

The framework is flexible with respect to the choice of Riemannian metric (Euclidean, pullback, pullback of an explicit data-manifold metric, and a KL-based approximation for probabilistic decoders), making it broadly applicable across different autoencoder types.

The learned denoising-based projection (Section 4) is autoencoder-agnostic and decouples the implicit-manifold representation from the specific network architecture, which is a clean and reusable design choice.

Experimental validation spans a genuinely diverse set of settings: discrete shells/isometric autoencoders, spherical VAEs on motion-capture data, low-distortion image autoencoders, and neural distance functions (Pose-NDF), showing the method generalizes across latent manifold types.

Extensive and thoughtful appendix comparisons against relevant prior art (Stochman parametric geodesics, Arvanitidis et al.'s uncertainty-regularized/RBF approaches, LAND density-based metrics) that discuss conceptual and computational trade-offs, and report timing information, adding useful context for the community.
Substantial implementation detail (network architectures, optimization hyperparameters, data generation procedures) is provided in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Most main-text results rely on qualitative visual comparisons (decoded image/pose sequences) rather than quantitative metrics (e.g., path energy, geodesic distance error, self-intersection rate); quantitative comparisons appear only sparingly in the appendix (e.g., the torus vs. Stochman comparison), limiting the strength of the empirical claims.

No explicit theoretical or empirical error bounds are given for how the accuracy of the learned approximate projection ζ_σ propagates to the accuracy of the computed discrete geodesics/exponential maps; the convergence guarantee cited (Rumpf & Wirth, 2015) only holds for the exact ζ.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters such as σ, network architecture, and augmented-Lagrangian penalty schedule appears substantial (Fig. 10, 11) and is only addressed with heuristic rules of thumb, which may hinder practical adoption without careful per-dataset tuning.

Robustness limitations are acknowledged but only briefly explored (e.g., exponential-map divergence in negatively curved regions in Fig. 4/15); a more systematic study of failure modes would strengthen the soundness claims.

Experiments are conducted on relatively small/synthetic or moderate-scale datasets (e.g., 71-shape SCAPE dataset, toy tori, synthetic point clouds); despite motivating references to large modern generative models (e.g., diffusion latents), no experiment demonstrates scalability to such high-dimensional, large-scale latent spaces.

Computational cost of the augmented Lagrangian optimization (seconds to minutes per geodesic/exponential map, per the appendix) is only reported informally and not systematically benchmarked against alternatives in the main text, leaving scalability to larger K, higher latent dimension, or batched geodesic queries unclear.

strengths: The paper builds on a rigorous mathematical foundation (Rumpf & Wirth's time-discrete geodesic calculus) and carefully extends it to the practically important case of imperfect, implicitly-defined latent manifolds, giving explicit discrete formulations for geodesic interpolation (augmented Lagrangian) and geodesic extrapolation (discrete exponential map).

The proposed denoising-based projection learning (Sec. 4) is autoencoder-agnostic and supports multiple choices of Riemannian metric on the latent space (Euclidean, pullback, application-specific), which is a flexible and reusable design.

The related-work section is unusually thorough and situates the contribution precisely with respect to a large body of prior latent-geometry work (Arvanitidis et al., Shao et al., Chen et al., Sun et al., etc.).

Experiments span a genuinely diverse set of autoencoder types and data domains: discrete-shell isometric autoencoders, spherical VAEs on motion-capture SO(3) data, low-distortion image autoencoders, and a neural pose-manifold distance function (Pose-NDF) — showing the method is not tailored to a single architecture.

Appendix C provides valuable quantitative/comparative analysis against existing tools (Stochman, Arvanitidis et al. 2018/2019/2022, LAND) including runtime, path energy, and robustness (e.g., divergence of exponential maps in negative curvature regions), going beyond purely qualitative figures.

The toy-model studies (torus, half-circle) with access to ground-truth implicit representations allow a sanity check of the method's approximation quality as a function of sample size, architecture, and noise level (Fig. 11).
weaknesses: Most of the main-paper results (Figs. 5–9, 12–14) are purely qualitative visual comparisons (linear vs. geodesic interpolation); there is no quantitative metric (e.g., manifold-adherence error, self-intersection rate, downstream task performance) reported for these real-data experiments, making it hard to assess the magnitude of improvement objectively.

The theoretical guarantees (e.g., Rumpf & Wirth's convergence result) apply only to the case of an exact, smooth implicit representation ζ; no formal analysis is given for how errors in the learned approximate projection Π_σ propagate to errors in the computed discrete geodesics/exponential maps beyond empirical illustration.

The method depends sensitively on the hyperparameter σ (noise scale for the denoising objective), with only qualitative guidance ('similar point cloud densities use the same σ') for choosing it in practice; no principled or automatic selection procedure is proposed.

The core technical contribution is largely a careful combination of two existing ingredients (Rumpf–Wirth discrete geodesic calculus and Alain–Bengio denoising-based projection learning), applied to the new setting of latent manifolds; the novelty is more in adaptation/engineering than in fundamentally new theory or algorithms.

The exponential map is shown to be numerically unstable and diverge quickly in regions of negative curvature (Fig. 4, Fig. 15), which is an important limitation for the extrapolation use-case the paper advertises, and is only briefly acknowledged rather than mitigated.

Scalability to high-dimensional or large-scale modern generative latent spaces (e.g., diffusion model latents, which are mentioned in the introduction as motivation) is not empirically demonstrated; all tested latent dimensions are modest (10–84), leaving open whether the approach is practical for large-scale generative models.

The augmented Lagrangian / BFGS-based optimization pipeline required for each geodesic computation appears computationally nontrivial (multiple seconds to minutes per example, per the appendix comparisons), and the paper does not clearly benchmark overall computational overhead against simpler baselines for the main real-data experiments (only for toy models in Appendix C).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of (i) learning an implicit representation of the latent manifold via a denoising/projection objective and (ii) a time-discrete variational geodesic calculus (building on Rumpf & Wirth, 2015) that computes both geodesic interpolation and the discrete exponential map without requiring an explicit parametrization of the manifold.

The framework is autoencoder-agnostic and flexible with respect to the choice of Riemannian metric (Euclidean, pullback, pullback of an explicit data-manifold metric, KL/Fisher-Rao based for probabilistic decoders), which is demonstrated concretely across several very different settings.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation: discrete shells/SCAPE with an isometric autoencoder, motion-capture data with a spherical VAE, image data of a rotating object with a low-distortion autoencoder, and an external neural distance function (Pose-NDF), in addition to carefully designed synthetic/toy examples (torus, rotated letter 'A') that permit comparison to ground truth.

Thoughtful, substantive comparisons to related numerical approaches (Stochman library, Arvanitidis et al.'s LAND and uncertainty-regularized decoder geodesics, density-based metrics) in the appendix, including runtime and qualitative robustness discussion (e.g., exponential map instability in negatively curved regions), which situates the contribution clearly relative to prior art.

A dedicated ablation (Appendix A.3) studying how the learned projection's accuracy depends on point-cloud size, network architecture, and noise level sigma, lending some empirical grounding to the method's sensitivity to hyperparameters.

Clear writing with an honest discussion of limitations and concrete directions for future work (e.g., connecting projection- and distance-based representations, extending to latent distributions, parallel transport, curvature).
weaknesses: Evidence is overwhelmingly qualitative/visual (side-by-side decoded sequences) rather than quantitative; aside from the toy torus and a couple of runtime/energy numbers in the appendix comparisons, there is no systematic quantitative metric (e.g., path energy, deviation from a reference geodesic, downstream task performance) reported across the main real-data experiments, making it hard to judge the magnitude of improvement objectively.

No formal error analysis or bound is given for the case of an inexact learned implicit representation zeta_sigma (as opposed to the known convergence result for exact, smooth zeta cited from Rumpf & Wirth); the robustness claims rest mainly on illustrative figures (e.g., Fig. 3/4) rather than theory or systematic quantitative error curves on real data.

Scalability to higher latent dimensions typical of modern large-scale generative models (e.g., hundreds to thousands of latent dimensions, as in diffusion model latents mentioned in the introduction) is not demonstrated; the largest latent dimension tested (l=84 for Pose-NDF) is still modest, leaving open questions about computational cost and projection quality at scale.

The method depends on several hyperparameters (sigma for the denoising projection, augmented Lagrangian tolerances/penalties, network architecture) that are tuned per experiment with limited systematic guidance beyond qualitative rules of thumb, which may hinder reproducibility and out-of-the-box applicability.

Some comparisons to baselines (e.g., Arvanitidis et al. 2022's sigmoid-based approach failing to converge in Fig. 16) are reported somewhat briefly without extensive tuning details for the baseline, raising a mild concern about whether the comparison is fully fair.

The real-data experiments (SCAPE with 71 shapes reduced to 1250 vertices, CMU mocap subset, a single rotating cow object) are relatively small-scale and somewhat specialized to geometry-processing/shape-space applications, which may limit the immediate significance of the contribution to the broader ICML audience interested in generative modeling or representation learning at scale.
